newsitem.title: INDIA: India mulls steps to boost offshore debt issues.
newsitem.headline: India mulls steps to boost offshore debt issues.

text.p: Indian firms and banks on Wednesday said an official panel's recommendations to make the rupee convertible on the capital account within three years would whet the country's rising appetite for offshore debt.
"This is the kind of flexibility the market wanted," Rana Kapoor, general manager, corporate finance and capital markets at ANZ Grindlays Bank, said on Wednesday.
"This will stimulate demand for offshore debt," he said.
Kapoor said the Indian offshore debt market had become deeper with more than 300 firms tapping cheaper offshore debt.
The committee on capital account convertibility recommended that the restrictions on the end use of foreign debt be lifted during the first phase of reforms in 1997/98 (April-March).
Also, the annual ceiling on external commercial borrowings set by the government should not apply to loans above 10-year maturity, the committee recommended.
In the second phase (1998/99), the panel said loans above seven years maturity should be taken out of the annual ceiling.
External commercial borrowings (ECBs) this year are expected to match last year's figure of close to $8.0 billion, bankers said.

Indian borrowers who contract an offshore dollar loan face two kinds of risks -- the prospect of dollar appreciation against major currencies and the risk of rupee depreciation during the repayment period.
"Looking at the appetite for ECB, it appears corporates are confident about the rupee's stability," said N.S. Paramasivam, head of the forex operations of India's private Essar Group.
Bankers said Indian firms could borrow at effective rates of 8.0 to 10.0 percent overseas compared to 14.0-15.0 percent at home, giving a spread of about four percent.
"People are confident about the rupee's stability in the near term, but not for seven years (the duration of a typical offshore loan)," Essar's Paramasivam said.
"The reward (of cheaper rate) is because of the risk."
Bankers said even hitherto conservative state-run firms were now tapping offshore debt with gusto.
"For many companies, exports provide a natural hedge," said a treasurer.
The charm of offshore debt is unlikely to weaken despite a fall in Indian interest rates in recent months, bankers said.
"I expect top corporates now taking seven year loans to graduate to longer tenures," said a banker.

A rise in ECBs and other forms of capital inflows and a slowdown in Indian imports has led to oversupply of dollars in the inter-bank foreign exchange market, prompting the rupee's appreciation in recent months.
The Reserve Bank of India has attempted to brake the rupee's rise by buying dollars but its intervention has been constrained by the expansion of domestic money supply.
